Le décès de Nooran, un jeune de 15 ans a: The death of Nooran, a 15-year-old shot by an officer of the Service de police de l'agglomération de Longueuil (SPAL) while unarmed, has sent a shockwave across Quebec. Through the voices of his friends and community workers, this article tells the story of the aftermath: the grief, the growing fear of police, the demand for justice, but also a broader questioning of the very role of this institution.
« Je n’arrive plus à manger. […] Je n’ar: “I can’t eat anymore. […] I can’t sleep either. It’s really hard for me,” says Mehdi, swaying his body from side to side as if trying to hold back an overflow of emotion. He says these words a few metres from the spot where his best friend, Nooran Rezayi, 15, fell under the bullets of a Longueuil police officer. On Sunday, September 21, a 911 call reporting a group of youths perceived as suspicious led to tragedy: Nooran, an unarmed teenager, was killed by two bullets. The act has left people bewildered and distraught. In the neighbourhood, in families, among Nooran’s friends, the same words keep coming back: brutality, fear, injustice. And a shared need: to understand. Why do police resort to such force? And how do we break the silence and impunity that make everything start over again and again? A report.
Non loin du croisement des rues Joseph-D: Not far from the intersection of Joseph-Daigneault and de Monaco streets, the asphalt has become a makeshift altar. Candles are lined up, bouquets pile up, stuffed animals keep watch over photos of Nooran placed here and there. Mehdi has come back every day since Sunday. “I wouldn’t wish going through this on anyone, really,” the teenager says. He could have been there during the police intervention. “He had invited me to come just chill with friends. But I had something else to do,” he continues, incredulous as he thinks about last Sunday’s tragic outcome.
Les souvenirs de Nooran remontent. Ryan: Memories of Nooran come flooding back. Ryan remembers Nooran as a endearing, radiant teenager: “He was smiling. He was really innocent, always positive. He wasn’t a violent person.”
Hanni, assis sur un bord de trottoir, ex: Hanni, sitting on a curb, says he feels as though he’s lived through an earthquake because of the violent circumstances of Nooran’s death. “Sunday and Monday, I was devastated. When I first heard the news, I didn’t believe it.” The shock came in waves: he couldn’t sit through a class at school, and couldn’t make sense of what had just happened. “They shot a 15-year-old. He was harmless. He didn’t have a weapon,” Hanni says indignantly.
En réponse à l’émoi de la communauté, le: In response to the community’s distress, the Service de police de l'agglomération de Longueuil (SPAL) says it has begun meetings with its partners, including school service centres and youth organizations.
« Ces échanges visent à mieux comprendre: “These discussions aim to better understand young people’s concerns, state of mind and feelings, while respecting everyone’s pace. It is a sincere effort to maintain trust and build lasting bridges with the community.”
Ce drame nourrit, chez les dizaines de j: For the dozens of young people gathered here, this tragedy feeds a chilling feeling: any one of them could be the victim of a police officer’s bullets. “The fact that he died in such a tragic way affects everyone who came here. It’s proof that young people, right now, can’t really be safe in Longueuil,” says Ryan, who adds that this fear is felt even within his family. “My parents are worried,” continues Ryan, who says he considered Nooran his little brother.
La mort de Nooran modifie de façon impor: Nooran’s death has profoundly changed their relationship with the police. “Honestly, I don’t feel safe,” Ryan says. He says he has already crossed paths with the same officer who fired: “Even when we cooperated, he didn’t respect what we said. He just wanted to put us in the wrong.”
Cette peur bouleverse le sens même de la: This fear upends the very meaning of safety. Where a patrol car should be reassuring, it becomes a source of anxiety. “They killed an unarmed, innocent child. When I see a police car, I’d rather walk away, because they’re going to do the same thing they did to Nooran,” believes Yassine. For these young people, the flashing lights and the uniform are no longer symbols of protection, but reminders of danger.
Tous perçoivent de l’injustice dans la m: All of them perceive injustice in their friend’s death. Mehdi sums up the feeling: “No matter what you do, even if you do nothing, some police officers can put you in danger.” He adds: “Firing a first bullet, already… but firing a second one, that’s really to shoot down and murder the victim.”
Et cette indignation gagne aussi les fam: This outrage is spreading to families as well. Moustapha Tamani, the father of one of Nooran’s friends, makes no secret of his bewilderment: “I think he was trigger-happy, as they say.” In his view, there are obvious facts about the scene that can’t simply be brushed aside, notably that the intervention took place in broad daylight. “Visibility was clear. An experienced officer could still see whether he had a weapon. I didn’t understand why fire two bullets at a young boy who was just trying to live. He was so cheerful, handsome, intelligent.”
D’après des témoignages que M. Tamani a: According to accounts Tamani gathered from the young people, Nooran was shot after trying to open his bag to show that he had no weapon. “That’s when he took a bullet in the stomach. […] And then they added the second bullet, which was fatal,” he says. For him, one detail remains incomprehensible: “The only weapon seized was the officer’s.”
Interrogé sur les circonstances de l’int: Asked about the circumstances of the intervention and the use of lethal force, the SPAL stated in an email: “No questions about the police intervention will be addressed for the moment, given that an independent investigation is currently underway.”
M. Tamani estime que ce n’est pas un inc: Tamani believes this is not an isolated incident, but the symptom of a deeper problem: “If we’ve gotten to the point where a child or a group of youths is a nuisance, and police show up and shoot at them...” After 25 years living in the neighbourhood, he says he is thinking of leaving. “I admit, walking around in a group of 15, 20, it makes noise. It bothered me too, sometimes. But they have the right to live, the right to be happy. This wasn’t a criminal group: the police knew them, but only for noise or minor neighbourhood calls.”
Puis, il insiste sur l’absurdité de la s: He then stresses the absurdity of the situation: “Just because you get a call doesn’t mean they’re armed and that you have to show up with guns and start shooting at children. A child, you fire in the air, he’ll be scared. He’ll stop,” he says, before addressing the police force directly. “Please, police, we love you, but don’t shoot our children. Stop killing our children.”
Pour le réalisateur et militant Will Pro: For filmmaker and activist Will Prosper, the news of Nooran Rezayi’s death first resonates as an intimate pain. “What’s most violent is his age: 15. I thought of my son too, who is 14. How can an unarmed young person get killed by the police?” he asks. In his voice, you hear both the instinctive fear of a father and the weariness of an activist. “Sadly, it’s history repeating itself again. We find ourselves playing ‘Groundhog Day.’”
Cette répétition, Prosper la connaît tro: Prosper knows this repetition all too well. His new short film, ReXistence, draws on this tragic mechanism. The timing of its release is unsettling. On Monday, September 22, as the press announced Nooran’s death, the National Film Board of Canada screened the 10-minute film that very evening. When the lights go down in the theatre, an explosion of archival images collide relentlessly, tracing decades of police brutality and racial discrimination against Black people, before rehumanizing the battered bodies by giving them back their history, their culture and their roots. Will Prosper stands by his choice of a hard-hitting edit which, he says, recreates the panic of being stopped: “When the flashing lights come on behind you, you never know what can happen.”
Une incertitude qui, au fil des décennie: Over the decades, that uncertainty has been associated with the faces of Anthony Griffin, Fredy Villanueva and Nicholas Gibbs, all killed by police fire. That is why the screening of ReXistence took on the feel of a cruel mirror, one in which past and present blur together. “How is it that the same story keeps going? That absolutely nothing is being done about it?” Will Prosper exclaims.
Il cite les recommandations faites après: He cites the recommendations made after Anthony Griffin’s death, the commission on racism in the taxi industry, and the coroner’s inquests into Fredy Villanueva and Marcellus François. “All those reports have been shelved,” he hammers home. “Police have blood on their hands because they can’t be bothered to apply solutions that are already written down in multiple reports!”
Et derrière cet immobilisme, Will Prospe: And behind this inertia, Will Prosper denounces a mechanism that blocks any change: omertà. “When a police officer commits racial profiling, it should be treated as a criminal offence. But in police culture, nobody talks. Those who see abuses keep quiet, for fear of reprisals.” This code of silence doesn’t only affect officers: it also weighs on victims and witnesses, who sometimes withdraw after providing evidence, fearing pressure.
La conséquence, dit-il, c’est une confia: The consequence, he says, is broken trust. And he points to a striking number: Nooran’s death led to the opening of the BEI’s 467th investigation since its creation in 2013. But in more than 10 years, there has not been a single conviction, he maintains.
L’avocat de la famille Rezayi, Mᵉ Fernan: The Rezayi family’s lawyer, Fernando Belton, does not mince words when discussing the record of the Bureau des enquêtes indépendantes (BEI). “The figure of zero [...] convictions hits hard in people’s minds.” He compares this with police ethics cases, of which only 1 to 3 per cent of files result in a citation. “In police ethics, year in and year out, 97 or 98 per cent of files will never make it to a tribunal. Who benefits from such leniency?” he asks.
À ses yeux, le message envoyé à la popul: In his view, the message sent to the public is clear: impunity. “If every time a person is killed, or a judgment finds racial profiling, there are no consequences, then we’re sending the message that you can keep acting this way.”
Sans aller jusqu’à conclure que la mort: Without going so far as to conclude that Nooran’s death is a case of racial profiling, he says the question is legitimate, before adding: “Why was there a need to use a weapon? And why target this group of young boys?”
Pour Mᵉ Belton, ces réflexes s’enracinen: For Belton, these reflexes are rooted in ideas inherited from the Code noir. “The conflation of racialized people in a group with danger goes back to slavery. In the Code noir, slaves were already forbidden to gather, to assemble at night, for fear they would organize a revolt. Today, when those stereotypes are internalized by those who hold authority, it leads to more brutal, faster interventions. And that is exactly the definition of racial profiling.”
L’avocat critique également la formulati: The lawyer also criticizes the wording used by the Bureau des enquêtes indépendantes in its communications: “The BEI spoke of a ‘seized weapon,’ when it was the officer’s weapon. It’s not a seized weapon, it’s the evidence of what killed Nooran.”
Pour Ted Rutland, professeur de géograph: For Ted Rutland, an urban geography professor at Concordia University and a specialist in policing policy, we must stop seeing the police as a neutral bulwark. “Historically, the police were created to protect private property and maintain an unequal social order, by targeting the poor and racialized people. It’s a lie to believe they exist to protect us.”
Cette logique explique, selon lui, la ré: This logic, he says, explains the repetition of tragedies and the near-total absence of sanctions. “The last time a police officer in Greater Montréal lost his job for killing someone was in 1988, after Anthony Griffin’s death. And he was reinstated a year later.”
Les caméras corporelles, souvent présent: Body cameras, often presented as a solution, are for him nothing but a “false good idea.” “They were designed to surveil the population, not to reform the police. Research shows they reduce neither racial profiling nor violence, and don’t increase the chances of sanctions. In Montréal, four police killings were filmed – those of Alain Magloire, Nicholas Gibbs, Pierre Coriolan and Abisay Cruz – without any consequences following,” says Professor Rutland. If the Fraternité promotes them, he continues, “it’s for the image and to create police jobs: a propaganda tool, not a tool of accountability.”
La véritable sortie de crise, dit-il, se: The real way out of the crisis, he says, lies elsewhere. “About 80 per cent of 911 calls have nothing to do with crime or violence. Why send experts armed with the use of force where a weapon isn’t needed?” He argues instead for “reducing the role of police, funding unarmed civilian responses and investing in prevention.”
Face à ce qu’il appelle un « manque de c: Faced with what he calls a “lack of political courage,” Rutland urges people to go beyond outrage: “In Montréal, we know how to protest, but governments are learning to ignore us. We also need to build networks of mutual aid and community safety, and be able to act politically against elected officials who don’t want to listen.”
« C’est arrivé le lendemain d’une confér: “It happened the day after a conference where I spoke about police brutality,” says Ricardo Lamour, a social worker, artist and longtime activist against police violence. Nooran’s death, he says, plunged him back into a far too familiar cycle: “It brings me back to a feeling of failure.” Other names resurface in his memory: Fredy Villanueva in 2008, Abisay Cruz this past March, Ronnie Kay in 2022.
Pour lui, il ne s’agit pas d’une bavure,: For him, this is not a blunder, but a machine working exactly as it is meant to. “Everything works with the police. The police are the arm of the state. They do what they’ve been mandated to do.” He cites Bill 14 of 2023, which restricted citizens’ recourse against police ethics violations. “Nooran’s friends, the neighbours, could have filed a complaint in the past. That right, they’ve lost it. I find that serious.”
Surtout, le militant insiste sur la méca: Above all, the activist insists on the very mechanics of the intervention: “It’s as if it’s the gaze that kills. Someone said: ‘I think those youths are armed.’ The police killed one of them.” A simple erroneous report was enough to set off the cascade of events.
Il fait apparaître un important contrast: He draws a striking contrast by recalling the arrest in Québec City in the summer of 2025 of four men suspected of belonging to an anti-government militia. At their homes, the RCMP found firearms, ammunition and cartridges. “They were arrested gently, without a single shot fired. How is it that, for an unfounded report, we end up with the death of a 15-year-old?”
À partir de ce constat, il élargit sa ré: From this observation, he broadens his reflection. “Quebec society must understand that its mere gaze, its mere anxiety, its mere fear of certain communities can lead to death.” He invokes the memory of Emmett Till, the young Black boy lynched at 14 in 1955 in the United States after being accused of looking at a white woman. “A simple look that leads to a report, that leads to an intervention. This is not a matter of good or bad police officers. It’s a matter of the system.”
